subject: mathematics
question_text: Using P.M.I, show that 2·4⁽²ⁿ⁺¹⁾ + 3⁽³ⁿ⁺¹⁾ is divisible by 11, ∀ n ∈ N.

verification.note: Source: Baby Bullet-Q, Junior Inter Maths-1A (Sri Publishers, Machilipatnam), book p.21 — the PRACTICE question printed at the foot of LAQ chapter 2. IMPORTANT: the book poses this question but gives NO worked solution and NO mark split, so unlike every other question in this unit BOTH the solution and the 1+1+1+3+1 split are ours — the split copied from the chapter's solved questions, the working done and checked here (n=1 gives 209 = 11 × 19; the step turns on 16 − 27 being a multiple of 11). No appearance years are printed. Everything here needs a teacher's confirmation. SUPERSEDED 2026-08-31 by the RE-CUT sentence at the end of this note — re-cut to the 8-mark Section-C form of the 2026-27 pattern (TGBIE model paper w.e.f. 2026-27): the extra mark goes to Step 3 — S(k+1) follows. RE-CUT 2026-08-31: this card was filed as LAQ at 8 marks and is now SAQ at 4 marks. The original label came from the Baby Bullet-Q blueprint for the superseded 75-mark paper; the Sri Chaitanya FAST TRACK IPE for Jr. Students — Mathematics-IA (2026-27 edition) prints this chapter under a Short Answer Questions banner and prints no long-answer block for it at all. Only the question was taken from a source book; the solution, the step order and the mark split are this answer book's own work — see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. The mathematics and the steps are unchanged; only the mark scheme moved — the four induction moves (base case, hypothesis, inductive step, conclusion) now carry 1 mark each and the opening statement step carries 0. Still unverified until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it.

recall_prompt: Say how you would prove this by induction — how each power grows, and which subtraction produces the 11.

steps.label: Write the statement
steps.margin_note: Unmarked setup at 4 marks, but never skip it — same first move as every divisibility proof: turn the word into an equation.

recall.must_convey: That divisible by 11 is written as the expression equalling 11q for an integer q.
accept: write it as equal to eleven q with q an integer
divisible by eleven means eleven times an integer
set the expression equal to eleven q
eleven q ki equal ga rastam

steps.why: 'Divisible by 11' is a phrase, and a phrase cannot be substituted into algebra. Writing it as = 11q, with q an integer, is what makes every later step possible.
common_mistakes: Reading 2·4 as the decimal two point four.
steps.memory_tip: Turn 'divisible by 11' into an EQUATION: equal to 11q with q an integer. Nothing can be substituted otherwise.

steps.label: Check S(1)
steps.margin_note: One mark. Work out both powers at n = 1 and name the multiple of 11.
lines: which is divisible by 11. So S(1) is true.

recall.must_convey: That at n = 1 the value is 2(64) + 81 = 209, and that 209 = 11 × 19.
accept: two times sixty four plus eighty one is two hundred nine which is eleven times nineteen
at n equals one you get two zero nine a multiple of eleven
four cubed is sixty four and three to the fourth is eighty one giving two zero nine
n equals one ki two zero nine vasthundi eleven into nineteen

steps.why: Naming 209 as 11 × 19 is what the examiner marks — 'divisible' on its own is an assertion.
common_mistakes: Exponent slip: at n = 1, 2n+1 is 3 and 3n+1 is 4.
steps.memory_tip: At n = 1 the powers are 4³ and 3⁴: 128 + 81 = 209 = 11 × 19. Name the multiple.

steps.label: Assume S(k) is true
steps.margin_note: One mark. Assume for k, number the line, and rearrange to isolate the first power — that is what Step 3 substitutes.
lines: Step 2 — assume S(k) is true, k ∈ N

recall.must_convey: That the statement is assumed for one k as 2·4⁽²ᵏ⁺¹⁾ + 3⁽³ᵏ⁺¹⁾ = 11q, and rearranged to give 2·4⁽²ᵏ⁺¹⁾ = 11q − 3⁽³ᵏ⁺¹⁾.
accept: assume it for k then make two times four to the two k plus one the subject
suppose s of k holds and rearrange to isolate the first term
take it as true for k and write the first power in terms of q
k ki assume chesi first term ni subject ga rastam
reject: let it be true for k

steps.why: Isolating one power means Step 3 substitutes once and leaves a single leftover term to collect.
common_mistakes: Rearranging for the wrong power, which makes the last step messier.
steps.memory_tip: Assume for k, number the line, and rearrange to isolate the FIRST power — that is what Step 3 substitutes.

steps.label: Show S(k+1) follows
steps.margin_note: One mark, and the longest step on the page. The powers grow by 4² = 16 and 3³ = 27. Substitute the rearranged line and collect — 27 − 16 = 11 is what finishes it.

recall.must_convey: That the first power grows by 16 and the second by 27, that (1) replaces 2·4⁽²ᵏ⁺¹⁾ by 11q − 3⁽³ᵏ⁺¹⁾, and that 27 − 16 = 11 leaves a factor of 11.
accept: the first term picks up sixteen and the second twenty seven then substitute and twenty seven minus sixteen is eleven
after substituting you get eleven times sixteen q plus three to the three k plus one
twenty seven minus sixteen equals eleven which is why it factors
twenty seven minus sixteen eleven kabatti factor avuthundi
heard_as: three to the three k plus one

steps.why: 27 − 16 = 11 is the hidden reason the question was chosen. Every divisibility proof of this shape is built around one such difference.
common_mistakes: Growth factors wrong: 4⁽²ᵏ⁺³⁾ is 16 × 4⁽²ᵏ⁺¹⁾ and 3⁽³ᵏ⁺⁴⁾ is 27 × 3⁽³ᵏ⁺¹⁾.
Substituting for both powers, leaving nothing to collect.
Not saying the final bracket is an integer.
steps.memory_tip: The powers grow by 4² = 16 and 3³ = 27, and 27 − 16 = 11 is exactly what finishes it.

steps.label: Conclude by P.M.I
steps.margin_note: The last mark is for naming the principle. One sentence, one mark.
lines: Hence, by the principle of finite

recall.must_convey: That S(1) is true and S(k) implies S(k+1), so by the principle of mathematical induction the statement holds for every natural number.
accept: since the first case is true and each case gives the next by p m i it is true for all n
hence by the principle of mathematical induction it holds for every natural number
base case plus inductive step gives it for all n in n
p m i prakaram anni n ki true

steps.why: The two proved statements are about n = 1 and about a step. Only the principle turns them into every n.
common_mistakes: Writing 'hence proved' without naming the principle.
steps.memory_tip: One sentence naming the principle is a whole mark. Write it.

insider_note: Rearrange the assumption to isolate the first term, 2·4^(2k+1) = 11q − 3^(3k+1), before substituting. The powers step up by 16 and 27, and 27 − 16 = 11 is precisely what makes the remainder vanish.
